references.text: The Mosaic law commands helping even your enemy's donkey—an early command to do good to those who hate you.
Proverbs encourages giving food and drink to an enemy, that is, doing good to those who hate you—the same principle as Jesus' command in Luke 6:27.
Jesus' parallel teaching in the Sermon on the Mount: "Love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you." A direct parallel to Luke 6:27.
Jesus further explains that loving only those who love you is nothing extraordinary—the rationale behind the command to love your enemies.
Paul exhorts: "Do not repay evil with evil... Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good." A direct elaboration of Jesus' command to love your enemies and do good to those who hate you.
Paul exhorts: "See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always pursue what is good for one another and for all." Reflects Jesus' command to do good to those who hate you.
Peter exhorts: "Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but on the contrary, bless." Expresses the same principle as Jesus' words about loving enemies and doing good.
Jesus himself as an example: He did not retaliate when he was reviled, nor threaten when he suffered—a practical example of doing good to those who hate you.
Stephen asks for forgiveness for those who are stoning him—a concrete example of loving your enemies and doing good to those who hate you.
